title: Intensive numerical tests with LANCELOT (Release A): the complete results
contribution: Archival report listing, for 943 CUTE problems and 21 LANCELOT algorithmic variants, the complete per-run minor iterations, gradient evaluations, cumulative CG iterations and CPU times on which the analysis paper [3] (Report 92/16) is based.
problem_entry: Not a new problem: the analysis in [3] could not list the many runs, so this report provides the complete results 'for future reference' (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: A four-metric grid (iterations, gradient evaluations, CG iterations, CPU seconds) over 943 problems x 21 variants, preceded by a problem-characteristics table with a cross-variant best objective value and followed by coded failures and bracketed wrong-minimum runs (pp. 2-3, 18-85).
assumptions: Problems (1)-(3) with smooth f and c, large n and/or m; runs capped at 1000 iterations, three million words of workspace and 18000 CPU seconds on a DECstation 5000/200; timings under f77 3.0-2 without optimization, rounded to seconds (pp. 2, 18, 69).
experiments: 943 CUTE instances (398 distinct names, n up to 15625), 21 variants, 4 cost measures; failure codes E/M/F/I/S/T; brackets flag >0.01% deviation from the best value; my tally: default 865/943 successful terminations, seprc 878, dfp 608; 920 problems solved by at least one variant, the 23 unsolved ones carry the best-value sentinel 0.1000000D+26 (pp. 3-34).
positioning: Cites only CUTE [1] (in preparation, 1992), the LANCELOT book [2] and the analysis report [3]; no comparison with other solvers inside the report (p. 86).
writing: Two short prose passages plus some 80 pages of tables; conventions stated once and reused ('Other conventions are as in the previous section'); variant definitions deliberately left to [3] (pp. 2, 18, 35, 52, 69).
limits_future: Variants undefined in the report; no separate function-evaluation count; no noisy or engineering tier; no summary statistics or profiles; no future directions stated (pp. 2-86).

method_links.note: Data layer of the LANCELOT testing twin: explicitly the basis of the discussion in [3], the numerical-experiments companion to the LANCELOT book.
Shared public collection (CUTE, 943 instances) and per-option reporting of all 21 variants including failures (Method 2 step 5).
Cost units are iterations, gradient evaluations, CG iterations and CPU time (derivative-based solver), not function evaluations; no noisy or engineering tier.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Per-run results for every problem x variant x measure published as a separate report so the analysis paper can stay short and every number stays checkable.

transferable: Publish a companion data report with every problem x variant x cost measure plus a problem-characteristics table (n, m, bound/constraint types, best value), and cite it from the analysis paper.
Code every failed run by cause (arithmetic error, memory, infeasible, iteration limit, tiny step, time limit) and count all of them as failures.
Flag runs that terminate successfully at a different objective value (relative tolerance 0.01% against the best value over all variants) instead of counting them as plain successes.
Report several cost units side by side and state machine, compiler, optimization level and timing rounding.

quotes.text: These results constitute the basis on the discussion and analysis presented by the authors in [3].
It is the purpose of the present report to provide, for future reference, the complete set of results on which this discussion is based.

title: Discontinuous piecewise differentiable optimization I: Theory
contribution: Introduces a decomposition of a (possibly discontinuous) piecewise linear function into a smooth part plus single-ridge terms, proves it exists and is unique at non-degenerate points, and derives from it per-activity optimality conditions and a finitely convergent active-set projected-gradient algorithm that generalizes Conn's 1973 l1 exact-penalty method, with a sketch of the nonlinear extension.
problem_entry: Generalize Conn's own l1 exact-penalty projection algorithm to general discontinuous piecewise linear problems (reduced to unconstrained form by the penalty (3)), motivated by VLSI/floorplanning, layout, batch production and fixed-charge applications and by the weaknesses of subgradient, bundle and smoothing methods (pp. 4, 6-7).
key_idea: Locally f(x) = f(x^) + g^T(x-x^) + sum_i v_i min(0, a_i^T(x-x^)) over active ridges (Definition 1, Theorem 1); a dead point is optimal iff g = sum u_i a_i with 0 <= u_i <= -v_i; descend by -Pg or by dropping one activity along +/-P_{-i}a_i with a breakpoint line search; for discontinuities use the lower semicontinuous envelope and ignore soaring directions, changing only step 4 (pp. 11-13, 22-24, 27, 35).
assumptions: Ridges, active sets and cell gradients available at any point (more than a bundle oracle); f decomposable at iterates and breakpoints; linearly independent active ridge gradients at dead points; non-contact points and known fault sets in the discontinuous case; degeneracy and contact points deferred to Part II (pp. 8, 11, 22, 31, 35).
proof_devices: change of variables y = Lx making active ridges coordinates; continuity forces cell-gradient components to depend only on sign(y_i), giving h(y) = y^T d^full + sum (d_i^empty - d_i^full) min(0, y_i) (pp. 14-15)
uniqueness by testing along single-dropping directions P_{-k} a_k (p. 16)
constructive decomposition from |A|+1 cell gradients instead of 2^|A| (Proposition 1, pp. 16-18)

finite termination by counting sign vectors sigma in {-1,0,1}^|R| that cannot recur under strict monotone decrease; active set grows at non-dead points, one activity dropped at dead points (Theorem 3, p. 26)
lower semicontinuous envelope turns infimum into minimum; soaring directions excluded so the continuous proofs carry over (pp. 27-28, 32-35)
experiments: none in Part I; implementation and numerical results deferred to Part II (pp. 4, 38)
positioning: Generalizes Conn 1973 [8], Conn-Pietrzykowski [14], Coleman-Conn [6,7] and shows Conn-Cornuejols facility location [11] as an instance with nested ridges; contrasts with subgradient/bundle methods, Fourer's piecewise-linear simplex and smoothing approaches (Zang, Imo-Leech) (pp. 6-7, 21, 24).
writing: Two-part paper announced in the abstract; one running toy example (the square-base pyramid (2)) reused for each definition; intuitive explanation placed before each proof; English and French abstracts (pp. 4-6, 10, 14, 18).
limits_future: Degeneracy, contact points, constrained case, implementation and numerics deferred to Part II; nonlinear extension only sketched with an expected linear rate for the first-order version; future comparison with bundle, composite nonsmooth methods and Clarke's theory (pp. 8, 36-38).

method_links.note: Conn's own 1973 l1 exact-penalty projection algorithm transplanted to discontinuous piecewise linear optimization; the Conn-Cornuejols facility-location method shown to be an instance.
Deliberately assumes and exploits more structure (ridges, cell gradients) than a bundle-method oracle; argues structure-exploiting nonsmooth methods beat general bundle methods.
Planned as paired publications from the start: Part I theory, Part II degeneracy, implementation and numerical results.

By analogy: a checkable geometric condition (linear independence of active ridge gradients) guarantees existence and uniqueness of the local model and carries the optimality theorem; degenerate case deferred.
Applications listed from the literature as motivation, not from a user engagement.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Nonsmooth function written locally as linear term plus one min(0,.) term per active kink, from which a per-kink multiplier interval test and single-dropping descent directions follow.
Discontinuous case handled by the lower semicontinuous envelope so that only step 4 of the algorithm changes and the decomposition/optimality proofs go through exactly as in the continuous case.

transferable: For a piecewise function, prove a canonical local form (linear part + sum v_i min(0, a_i^T(x-x^))) exists under a regularity condition, then derive the optimality test and descent directions one kink at a time.
Prove finite termination by showing iterates never revisit a sign pattern of the active constraints while f strictly decreases.
Handle discontinuities by working with the lower semicontinuous envelope and forbidding only directions along which f jumps up, keeping the rest of the continuous algorithm.
In an exact line search along a piecewise-linear path, pop breakpoints from a heap and update the directional derivative at each breakpoint instead of sorting all of them.

quotes.text: (Hence, we are assuming that more information on the structure of the objective function is available than, for example, in a bundle method, which assumes that only one element of the subdifferential is known at any point.)
We have hence set a framework for an algorithm dealing directly with discontinuities that could be involved in a non-differentiable optimization problem.

title: Global convergence of a class of trust region algorithms for optimization using inexact projections on convex constraints
contribution: Proves global convergence to critical points, finite identification of the binding (in)equality constraints and (under second-order sufficiency) whole-sequence convergence for a class of trust-region methods on convex feasible sets that allows iteration-dependent general norms, approximate gradients with error <= kappa*Delta_k and inexact projected-gradient (generalized Cauchy point) computations, e.g. by truncated LPs; also covers noisy function values.
problem_entry: Existing convex-constraint trust-region theories need the explicitly computed Euclidean projected gradient, which may be expensive; with polyhedral norms the projection becomes an LP that network and staircase structure make cheap (p. 3).
key_idea: Replace the projected-gradient Cauchy point by a Generalized Cauchy Point defined only through conditions (2.30)-(2.35): feasible, within nu2*Delta_k, achieving a fraction mu3 of the best linearized decrease chi_k(t) in a ball of radius t, plus Goldstein-type or length conditions; any step giving a fraction of the GCP decrease is accepted (pp. 9-11).
assumptions: Compact level set, Lipschitz gradient, uniformly equivalent norms, gradient error <= kappa1*Delta_k, divergent sum 1/beta_k of model curvature bounds, beta_k[f(x_k)-f(x_k+1)] -> 0; for identification also AS.6-AS.11 (LICQ, Dunn nondegeneracy, asymptotically exact gradients, admitted to simplify exposition); AS.12 (C2) for whole-sequence convergence (pp. 4, 6-7, 20, 22, 35-37, 48).
proof_devices: criticality measure chi_k[x] = |min <grad f, d>| over x+d in X, ||d||_(k) <= 1, proved equivalent across norms by sandwiching unit balls between two l2 balls (Theorem 4, pp. 13-14)
chi(t)/t nonincreasing via rescaling the t2-optimal step by t1/t2 and convexity of X (Lemma 2, p. 8)
Cauchy-type decrease m_k(x_k)-m_k(x_k+s_k) >= c3 chi_k min[1, Delta_k, chi_k/(1+omega_k^C)] with curvature along the step as a Rayleigh quotient (Theorem 9, pp. 17-18)
radius lower bound Delta_k >= c5/beta_k by contradiction at the first violating index (Lemma 12, pp. 19-20)
Powell's lemma: sum over successful k of min(Delta_k, eps/beta_k) finite implies sum 1/beta_k finite, contradicting AS.4 (Lemma 13, Theorem 14, p. 21)
liminf to lim via two interleaved subsequences m_i, l_i and AS.5 (Theorem 17, pp. 22-24)
LP weak-duality bound as stopping certificate for the inexact GCP linear program (7.12) (pp. 50-51)
relative noise ratio E_k = (f(x_k)-m_k(x_k))/(m_k(x_k)-m_k(x_k+s_k)) inserted into the rho_k bound of Lemma 12 (pp. 57-58)
two-variable constrained counterexample (7.28)-(7.29) showing a fixed relative gradient-accuracy condition (Carter) fails under constraints (pp. 54-55)
experiments: none; typical constant values listed, remaining constants 'will only become clear after extensive testing' (p. 13)
positioning: Extends CGT 1988 bound-constrained theory [9], Burke-More-Toraldo [4], More [20] and Toint [29] 'in a more general setting'; inexact-gradient device taken from Toint [29]; Carter's relative accuracy condition [6] shown insufficient under constraints; uses Dunn's nondegeneracy and Burke-More identification ideas (pp. 3, 37, 54-55).
writing: Bulleted list of new features in the introduction; numbered remarks motivating each algorithmic condition; 'familiar vocabulary of classical optimization' chosen over convex-analysis prerequisites; glossary and one-page assumption summary in appendices; long discussion-and-extensions section (pp. 3, 7, 10-13, 50-58, 62-66).
limits_future: GCP algorithm is only a feasibility model (inner solver, t0, special cases open); AS.9 and AS.11 strong; identification without LICQ only 'weak' and a geometric version is ongoing research; application to network flow-conservation constraints under study (pp. 28, 37, 53-54, 58).

method_links.note: Pre-DFO precursor: model accuracy is an explicit algorithm-independent condition ((2.13): gradient error <= kappa1*Delta_k) and convergence is proved once for any model satisfying (2.12)-(2.13) plus curvature conditions.
Workflow D step 1 made a theorem: with noisy f, convergence (Theorems 14, 17) survives if the ratio of function-value uncertainty to predicted model decrease stays below a modest bound (about 0.1).
Theory-only member of the triad: GCP procedure is only a model, constants left to extensive testing, network application still under study; Report 90/4 revised 1995.
Theory covers 'a relatively abstract algorithmic class' defined by conditions (taste #2), even covering linesearch methods.
Designed to exploit cheap null-space bases (network spanning trees, staircase matrices) via polyhedral norms and LPs.

Transplants the 1988 bound-constrained trust-region theory to general convex sets and imports LP machinery (simplex bases, weak duality, interior-point duality gaps) into the Cauchy-point computation.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: (2.12) is used only in Lemma 11, so noisy function values are handled by patching that one inequality; AS.6 results obtained by 'entirely similar' proofs with chi_k replaced by chi_k^C.
Exact projection replaced by a fraction-of-optimum condition on the linearized decrease, certified during a simplex solve by an LP weak-duality bound.

transferable: When a subproblem (projection onto X) is expensive, require only a fraction mu3 of the optimal linearized decrease chi_k(t) and certify it cheaply, e.g. stop a simplex method when <g,d_l> <= -mu3 * (best dual objective so far).

Let the norm vary by iteration and prove once that the criticality measures are uniformly equivalent (Theorem 4); the norm then becomes a free design choice such as l_inf or polyhedral norms that turn subproblems into LPs.

Make the accuracy requirement on approximate gradients proportional to the trust-region radius (||e_k|| <= kappa*Delta_k) rather than a fixed relative accuracy, and show with a small constrained example why the fixed version fails.
Before generalizing a convergence proof, list which lemma uses which assumption and extend by modifying only those lemmas (noisy f needs only a bound on noise / predicted decrease).
After the algorithm statement, add numbered remarks justifying each condition, and put every assumption in a one-page appendix.
coauthors: N.I.M. Gould, A. Sartenaer, Ph.L. Toint

quotes.text: Of course, this only describes a relatively abstract algorithmic class.
We emphasize that this GCP Algorithm is only a model, intended to show feasibility of our approach
